title: The serpent's question
teaser: The first lie did not deny God. It rephrased Him. Four words still rearrange faith into doubt: Did God really say?
framework: Genesis 3:1-7 — Deception by distortion. The serpent twists what God said, and the twist becomes the wound.

panels.heading: A QUESTION IN THE GARDEN
panels.content:
Day one began with a voice over the deep. Light, sky, sea, soil, every kind of life, each called good. A blessing was spoken over the people made in God's image, and rest settled on the seventh day.

Now another voice speaks. It is quieter. It does not announce itself. It asks a question.

**"Did God really say?"**

Four words. Not a denial. Not yet. Just a small tug on the thread of memory. The serpent does not begin with a lie about God. He begins with a question about what God said.

Notice where this lands. Not in the city. Not in the marketplace. In the garden. Inside the place that was supposed to be safe.

panels.heading: READ THE TEXT
panels.content:
Genesis 3:1-7 (BSB):

> "Now the serpent was more crafty than any beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, 'Did God really say, "You must not eat from any tree in the garden"?'
>
> The woman answered the serpent, 'We may eat the fruit of the trees of the garden, but about the fruit of the tree in the middle of the garden, God has said, "You must not eat of it or touch it, or you will die."'
>
> 'You will not surely die,' the serpent said to the woman. 'For God knows that in the day you eat of it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.'
>
> When the woman saw that the tree was good for food and pleasing to the eyes, and that it was desirable for obtaining wisdom, she took the fruit and ate it. She also gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate it. And the eyes of both of them were opened, and they knew that they were naked; so they sewed together fig leaves and made coverings for themselves."

Watch what the serpent does in three small moves.

First, omission. God had said they could eat from any tree except one. The serpent flips it: "You must not eat from any tree in the garden?" He shrinks God's generosity until it sounds like a fence.

Second, addition. Eve adds a phrase God never spoke: "or touch it." The command grows heavier in her mouth than it ever was in His. A small inflation, but it makes the rule feel cruel.

Third, suspicion. "God knows..." The serpent does not have to argue God's existence. He only has to whisper that God is holding out, that the heart behind the word is not love but jealousy.

The fruit comes last. The wound is already done before the bite.

panels.heading: WHERE DAY 1 ECHOES
panels.content:
Five days ago we read, "In the beginning, God." The opening note of Scripture is divine speech that brings order out of chaos. Word. Light. Naming. Blessing. Today the same created order is unmade by speech that distorts. The serpent does not invent a counter-creation; he editorializes the first one.

This is the *remez*, the hint the rest of the Bible will keep tracing. Every later seduction in Scripture follows this grammar. The golden calf is offered as the god "who brought you out of Egypt," God's own line mouthed by an idol. False prophets in Jeremiah preach peace where God has not promised peace. The accuser in Job suggests Job only loves God for the perks. The pattern is older than any of these. It begins in chapter three.

Now track it forward. In Matthew 4:1-11 another wilderness, another fast, another voice in the silence. "If you are the Son of God..." The tempter even quotes Psalm 91, distorting Scripture by lifting it free of its context. Where Eve answered with a phrase God never said, Christ answers three times with what God did say. **"It is written."** Not louder. Not cleverer. Just truer.

panels.heading: WHEN THE QUESTION SURFACES
panels.content:
The serpent's question still surfaces. It rarely arrives as open rebellion. More often it sounds reasonable, and it sounds like our own thought.

*Did God really say sex was meant for one covenant?*
*Did God really say to forgive again?*
*Did God really say He loved you, after the year you've had?*

The distortion is the same shape every time. A small omission. A small addition. A whisper of suspicion. Notice when the question arrives in your own head. The shape itself is a tell. You are not losing your mind. You are hearing something old.

The answer is not to argue louder. The answer is to return to what God actually said: read it, not paraphrased; remembered, not edited. Christ in the wilderness gives us the form: open the text, speak it back, refuse the rephrasing.

panels.heading: A PRAYER FOR DISCERNMENT
panels.content:
Father,

When "Did God really say?" surfaces in my own thinking today, give me ears to hear the shape of it. Show me where I have shrunk Your generosity into a fence, or added weight You never put on me, or believed You were holding out.

Teach me Christ's answer in the wilderness. Bring me back to what is written.

In Jesus' name. Amen.

endnotes.ref: Augustine of Hippo, *City of God*, Book XIV, Ch. 11–13 (426 AD), on the inward pride that preceded the outward act in Eden.
C. S. Lewis, *The Screwtape Letters* (Geoffrey Bles, 1942), Letter 4 — the tempter's preferred method is not denial but distortion.
